stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
After the city of Harlow Falls raised its minimum wage by 18 percent, economist Dalia Osei tracked staffing at 240 local restaurants. Eighteen months later, payroll head counts were essentially unchanged. Osei concluded that the higher wage floor had not reduced restaurants' use of low-wage labor.

Text 2
Osei's head counts are careful, and the restaurants did keep about as many people on staff. But a payroll lists a worker scheduled for twelve hours a week the same way it lists one scheduled for thirty, and the restaurants' time sheets show average weekly hours per employee falling by roughly a tenth.
choices: The wage increase did little to change how much low-wage labor the restaurants used.
The restaurants employed about as many workers after the increase as they had before it.
Payroll head counts cannot reveal how the restaurants adjusted to the higher wage.
Raising a city's minimum wage does not, in general, cause employers to cut jobs.
explanation: Text 1 sets up a finding (head counts stayed the same) and then draws a conclusion from it (the restaurants used no less labor). Text 2 opens by granting the finding ('the restaurants did keep about as many people on staff'). It then disputes only the conclusion, because hours per worker fell. So Text 2 qualifies Text 1. It accepts the observation and rejects the inference. The only thing both authors would accept is the observation itself: the restaurants employed about as many workers as before.

A.why: This is Text 1's final conclusion, and it is exactly what Text 2 was written to challenge. Fewer hours per worker means the restaurants used less labor even with the same head count. You saw that Text 2 concedes something, but you picked the claim it rejects instead of the one it concedes.

C.why: This gets Text 2's position right but not Text 1's. Osei relied on head counts as her evidence, so she would not accept that they miss how the restaurants adjusted. A statement that only one author holds cannot be something both would agree with.

D.why: This is a stronger version of Text 1's claim than Text 1 actually makes. Osei drew a conclusion about one city's restaurants, not about minimum wage increases in general. Text 2 also gives no support for a general rule. Neither author would sign on to a law about all employers.

subtype_name: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In the eleven days before a magnitude 5.4 earthquake struck the Vessel Ridge fault, seismometers recorded over 300 small tremors clustered near the eventual rupture. Geophysicist Tomas Reyna concludes that the tremors marked slow, silent slip that loaded the fault until it failed, and thus that swarms there may warn of larger shocks.

Text 2
The timing and placement of the Vessel Ridge tremors are hard to dismiss as chance. Yet fluid rising through fractured rock can raise pressure enough to set off a swarm and, days later, a larger rupture, and it is difficult to exclude that sequence. If fluid was responsible, a swarm need not reflect slow slip.
choices: The tremors reveal that slow slip was loading the fault before it ruptured.
Swarms on the Vessel Ridge fault reliably signal that a larger quake will follow.
The tremors were most likely connected to whatever produced the mainshock.
Rising fluid is the likelier source of the tremors recorded before the mainshock.
explanation: Text 1 gives an observation (a swarm of tremors just before and near the mainshock) and an explanation for it (slow slip loaded the fault). Text 2 offers a different explanation for the same observation: rising fluid could have caused both the swarm and the rupture. Text 2 does not deny the link between the swarm and the mainshock. It says the link is 'hard to dismiss as chance'. Reyna's account also ties the two together, through slow slip. The authors disagree about what the connecting cause was, but both treat the tremors as connected to the cause of the mainshock.

A.why: This is Reyna's explanation, and it is the very claim Text 2 targets. Text 2 says that if fluid was responsible, the swarm 'need not reflect slow slip.' You found the claim under attack but treated it as common ground.

B.why: This turns Text 1's claim into a stronger one than it makes. Reyna says swarms 'may warn' of larger shocks, not that they reliably do. Text 2's account suggests a swarm might show only that fluid is moving. Neither author makes a claim this strong.

D.why: This gets one text's role right and the other's wrong. Text 2 only says the fluid sequence is 'difficult to exclude'. It never says fluid is the likelier cause, and Reyna would reject the idea outright. Agreeing with a hedged alternative is different from both authors endorsing it.
